notes: Where the lidar and the two cameras sit relative to each other. HAND-MEASURED,
not fitted -- these are the numbers to edit when something is re-bolted, and
test/test_lidar_overlay.py is how you check them against a real image.
FRAME. Everything is expressed in the RIG frame, which uses the same axis
convention as the camera frame already on the wire (see protocol.py ray_cam):
+x starboard (right)   +y DOWN   +z forward
Note +y is DOWN, so a camera mounted above the lidar has a NEGATIVE y.
By default the rig frame is the lidar's own frame (the lidar pose below is all
zeros), because the mounting was measured from the lidar's centre. Give the
lidar a pose if you later define a boat datum somewhere else -- everything
downstream goes through the same transform either way.
POSE. Each entry is the pose of that body IN the rig frame:
p_rig = R(yaw,pitch,roll) @ p_body + xyz_m
Angles in degrees, applied yaw*pitch*roll (roll first):
yaw   about +y (down)     positive swings to STARBOARD
pitch about +x (right)    positive is NOSE UP
roll  about +z (forward)  positive puts STARBOARD DOWN
DEFAULTS. Cameras about horizontal, 15 deg either side of forward (30 deg
between them), each about 5 cm from the lidar centre along its own pointing
direction and about 5 cm above the scan plane -- the height is what stops the
camera body blocking the lidar. cam0 and cam1 are written out in full rather
than mirrored so each can absorb its own mounting error independently.
The cameras are inverted and the pipeline rotates 180 deg before anything else
sees the frame, so the calibration, the images and these poses are all in the
same upright frame. There is no extra flip to apply here.
SANITY. The lidar plane sits 5 cm below the lens, so returns land slightly
below the horizon row and converge onto it with range: at 0.5 m a return is
about 50 net px below the axis, at 3 m about 6, at 12 m under 2. If your
overlay shows the opposite trend, y has the wrong sign.

_yaw: The unit is bolted on rotated about 45 deg to the LEFT (to port), so its own
0 mark points 45 deg to port of the boat's forward. -45 here turns the scan
back onto the rig's axes, which is what makes a return dead ahead of the boat
come out at rig bearing 0 and line up with the cameras.
Check the sign before trusting it: with this right, an object straight ahead
reads near 0 deg in the overlay tool and near the top of the receiver's
top-down plot. If everything sits 90 deg out, the sign is flipped.
_angle: How the C1's reported heading becomes a direction in the rig frame:
so a = 0 is forward (+z) and a grows toward starboard (+x).
angle_dir is +1 for the C1's clockwise-from-above convention and -1 if your
unit or mounting runs the other way; angle_zero_deg rotates the sensor's own
0 mark onto the rig's forward. VERIFY BOTH with the overlay tool rather than
trusting them -- a sign error here looks like a plausible but mirrored world,
which is the failure most likely to survive a casual glance.
